newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam sentences "hard-core terrorists" to death.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam sentences "hard-core terrorists" to death.

text.p: Two people have been sentenced to death and three jailed for life on terrorism charges in southern Vietnam, an official said on Wednesday.

The official at the Ho Chi Minh City People's court told Reuters the five were members of a group involved in a grenade attack in a crowded city park in 1994 in which nearly 20 people, including 10 foreigners, were hurt.
He said the five were arrested in 1996 after two were caught trying to smuggle subversive documents into Vietnam from Cambodia.

The official Saigon Times Daily described them as "hard-core terrorists" and said they were part of a group led by anti-Vietnam exiles living in the United States and known as the "Vietnam Front for Regime Restoration".

It said their aim was to sabotage Vietnam's political, diplomatic and economic stability by waging a guerrilla campaign in which foreign investors were targeted, especially those from China, Taiwan and Hong Kong.
Most of those wounded in the 1994 incident, which took place on a wharf near the city's landmark Majestic Hotel, were ethnic Chinese.
Acts of subversion in Vietnam are rare, but the communist government is nonetheless concerned by groups that it says are bent on seeking its overthrow.

A number of those are made up of exiles living in third countries. In late 1995 Cambodia deported six U.S. citizens, including five ethnic Vietnamese, for an alleged plot to overthrow Vietnam's communist leaders.
Earlier that year, a Ho Chi Minh City court sentenced two Vietnamese-Americans and seven Vietnamese nationals to long jail terms for attempted subversion.
The current nationalities of the five men sentenced this week were not clear, although all are ethnic Vietnamese. The two sentenced to death were named as Tran Van Thuan, 29, and Huynh Te Cam, 39.

The Saigon Times Daily said the group had sent threatening letters to the city's Rex Hotel and an office of Japan's Mitsubishi Corporation. It said similar documents had been found in the United States and at Vietnam's embassy in Canada.
